title: Ezekiel 1:15–21
context: The prophet continues the vision begun in 1:4. Beside the living creatures he sees “one wheel on the earth” for each of the four faces (1:15). The wheels look “like a beryl”, are alike, and appear “as it were a wheel within a wheel” (1:16). They go in their four directions without turning, their rims are “high and dreadful” and “full of eyes all around”, and they rise and stop with the creatures, “for the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels” (1:17–21). The text describes how the wheels move but does not explain their construction or decode the eyes; this page keeps to its terms. Chapter 10 returns to the wheels in a later vision (compare 10:9–13). Many readers in both traditions see in this movement a sign that the LORD’s presence is not confined to the temple in Jerusalem. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: the whole scene moves as one under the spirit’s direction.

verses.text: Now as I saw the living creatures, behold, there was one wheel on the earth beside the living creatures, for each of the four faces of it.
verses.arminianNotes: Beside the living creatures the prophet sees “one wheel on the earth” for each. Arminian readers note that the vision now reaches the ground. The wheels touch the earth where the exiles are, while remaining part of the heavenly scene.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the wheels as part of a single throne-vision that reaches the earth. Shared ground: both traditions read the wheels descriptively, and neither turns them into a theological fork or gives them a fixed meaning the text does not supply.

verses.text: The appearance of the wheels and their work was like a beryl. The four of them had one likeness. Their appearance and their work was as it were a wheel within a wheel.
verses.arminianNotes: The wheels look “like a beryl” and appear “as it were a wheel within a wheel.” Arminian readers note that the prophet admits the limits of his description. Proposals about how such wheels were built go beyond the text, and readers do well to hold them loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress the “as it were” and decline to reconstruct the wheels mechanically. Shared ground: both traditions read the gleaming wheels as part of the brilliance of the LORD’s presence and let the description remain a description.

verses.text: When they went, they went in their four directions. They didn’t turn when they went.
verses.arminianNotes: “When they went, they went in their four directions.” Arminian readers often see here freedom of movement in every direction. Many take the vision to suggest that no place, including Babylon, lies beyond the reach of the LORD’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s presence able to move anywhere without hindrance, fitting his rule over all lands. Shared ground: both traditions read the unturning movement as a sign of the presence’s sure direction, and both hedge any further symbolism.

verses.text: As for their rims, they were high and dreadful; and the four of them had their rims full of eyes all around.
verses.arminianNotes: Their rims were “high and dreadful”, and “full of eyes all around.” Arminian readers often connect the eyes with the LORD’s all-seeing knowledge, while noting that the text does not explain them. The awe the prophet feels is the main point.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise often relate the eyes to God’s watchful knowledge, offering it as a reading rather than the text’s own explanation (compare 10:12). Shared ground: both traditions read the rims as dreadful and wondrous, and neither builds a contrast on the detail.

verses.text: When the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them. When the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up.
verses.arminianNotes: “When the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them.” When the creatures were lifted, the wheels were lifted. Arminian readers note the perfect coordination of the vision. Every part moves as one, with nothing out of step with the purpose that directs it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the whole scene moving in unity, ordered from above. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the vision’s description of movement, and both see a picture of creatures and wheels serving one purpose together.

verses.text: Wherever the spirit was to go, they went. The spirit was to go there. The wheels were lifted up beside them; for the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels.
verses.arminianNotes: “Wherever the spirit was to go, they went.” The wheels rose beside the creatures, “for the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels.” Arminian readers note that a single animating spirit unites the creatures and the wheels. The text stresses direction and unity, not mechanics.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see one directing spirit governing the whole vision. Shared ground: both traditions read the spirit’s direction as the source of the movement, and both leave open how closely to relate this spirit to the Spirit who lifts the prophet in 2:2 and 3:12, since the text does not say.

verses.text: When those went, these went. When those stood, these stood. When those were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up beside them; for the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels.
verses.arminianNotes: “When those went, these went. When those stood, these stood.” Arminian readers note that the repetition fixes the image in the reader’s mind. The prophet wants his hearers to grasp the unity of the moving glory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see emphasis through repetition, restating that “the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing the description of the wheels before the prophet looks up to the expanse and the throne in 1:22.
